concept.name: Moving-average crossover strategy
concept.definition: A trend-following rule that goes long when a short moving average crosses above a longer one and exits or shorts on the reverse cross, using the smoothed momentum of two lookback windows as the signal. It is the canonical moving-average rule in Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron's (1992) tests of simple technical trading rules.
concept.intuition: The short average is the market's recent mood, the long average its season; when mood crosses season something has changed - you trade the crossing, accepting that you will be late at both turns.
concept.mechanics: Compute a fast and a slow moving average; hold long while the fast average is above the slow one (golden-cross state) and flat or short while below (death-cross state), optionally with a band filter to suppress noise crosses. Brock-Lakonishok-LeBaron tested variable-length moving-average rules (e.g., 1/50, 1/150, 5/150, 1/200, 2/200) on the Dow from 1897 to 1986 with bootstrap comparisons.
concept.formula: SMA_N(t) = (1/N) sum_{i=0}^{N-1} P(t-i); signal = sign(SMA_fast - SMA_slow).
concept.failure_modes: In range-bound markets the crossovers whipsaw, entering at local extremes of each oscillation, and the rule's structural lag means V-shaped reversals cost the full round trip before the signal flips.
concept.misconceptions: That a golden cross is a validated buy signal; it is a descriptive trend-following framework whose historical test results are sample- and cost-dependent, not a proven predictive law.
concept.example: A 50-day SMA rising through the 200-day SMA at $98 flips the system long; it stays long until the 50-day falls back below the 200-day at $91, capturing the intervening trend less the lag at both ends.

citations.source: Brock, Lakonishok & LeBaron, 'Simple Technical Trading Rules and the Stochastic Properties of Stock Returns', Journal of Finance 47(5), 1992, 1731-1764 (EconPapers record)
